q: 1. When a thin cylindrical shell is subjected to internal fluid pressure, which of the following stress is developed in its wall ?
explain: Internal pressure in cylinders creates both hoop (circumferential) and longitudinal stresses.

q: 2. If a shaft subjected to pure torsion cracks, the crack will start
explain: Since shear stress due to torsion is maximum at the outer surface (periphery) and zero at the centre, cracks in a shaft under torsion initiate at the periphery.

q: 3. Shear strain theory for the failure of a material at elastic limit is due to
explain: The shear strain energy (distortion energy) theory of failure is attributed to Von Mises (also known as the Von Mises-Hencky theory).

q: 4. Gradually applied static loads do not change with time their
explain: A static load, by definition, is applied gradually and remains constant in magnitude, direction, and point of application over time — hence 'all of these'.

q: 5. The sum of normal stress is
explain: The sum of normal stresses on two mutually perpendicular planes at a point (σx + σy) is a stress invariant — it remains constant regardless of the orientation of the planes chosen.

q: 6. The radius of Mohr's circle for two equal unlike principle stresses of magnitude P is
explain: For two equal but unlike (opposite sign) principal stresses +P and −P, the radius of Mohr's circle = (σ1−σ2)/2 = (P−(−P))/2 = P.

q: 7. Shear stress on principal planes is
explain: By definition, principal planes are those on which shear stress is zero (only normal stress acts).

q: 8. The bending moment at a section tends to bend or deflect the beam and the internal stresses resist bending. The resistance offered by the internal stresses, to the bending, is called
explain: The internal resisting stress developed within a beam's cross-section to counter the external bending moment is termed bending stress.

q: 9. The neutral axis of the cross-section of a beam is that axis at which the bending stress is
explain: By definition, the neutral axis is the axis in the cross-section where bending stress (and strain) is zero.

q: 10. A beam of uniform strength may be obtained by
options: keeping the width uniform and varying the depth
keeping the depth uniform and varying the width
varying the width and depth both
explain: A beam of uniform strength can be achieved by varying depth alone, width alone, or both together, as long as the section modulus varies appropriately with the moment — hence any of these approaches works.

q: 11. At the neutral axis of a beam
options: the layers are subjected to maximum bending stress
the layers are subjected to minimum bending stress
the layers are subjected to compression
the layers do not undergo any strain
explain: Fibres along the neutral axis experience zero strain (neither elongation nor compression) during bending, by definition of the neutral axis.

q: 12. The neutral axis of a beam is subjected to ............. stress.
explain: Since strain at the neutral axis is zero, and stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law), the bending stress there is also zero.

q: 13. The neutral axis of a transverse section of a beam passes through the centre of gravity of the section and is
options: in the same plane in which the beam bends
at right angle to the plane in which the beam bends
explain: The neutral axis lies perpendicular to the plane of bending (the plane containing the applied loads and curvature), while passing through the section's centroid.

q: 14. In a beam subjected to pure bending, the intensity of stress in any fibre is ............. the distance of the fibre from the neutral axis.
explain: From the flexure formula σ = My/I, bending stress varies linearly (directly proportional) with distance y from the neutral axis.

q: 15. The ratio of maximum shear stress developed in a rectangular beam and a circular beam of the same cross-sectional area is
explain: Comparing the maximum shear stress factors of a rectangle (1.5×average) and circle (1.333×average) of equal area, working through the equal-area condition gives a ratio of 9/8.

q: 16. A beam of triangular section is placed with its base horizontal. The maximum shear stress occurs at
options: centre of gravity of the triangle
explain: For a triangular section with base horizontal, detailed analysis shows the maximum shear stress occurs at mid-height, not exactly at the centroid or base.

q: 17. Coefficient of wind resistance of a circular surface is
explain: The standard coefficient of wind resistance (pressure coefficient) for a circular (cylindrical) surface, as used in practical wind load calculations, is taken as 2/3.

q: 18. The ratio of circumferential stress to the longitudinal stress in the walls of a cylindrical shell due to flowing liquid is
explain: For a thin cylindrical shell under internal pressure, circumferential (hoop) stress = pd/2t while longitudinal stress = pd/4t, giving a ratio of 2:1.

q: 19. Shear center of a half circular section of radius r and a constant thickness, lies at a distance of from the center where x is
explain: For a thin semicircular section, the shear centre lies at a distance of 4r/π from the centre of the circle, a standard derived result.

q: 20. Euler's formula holds good only for
explain: Euler's buckling formula is derived assuming purely elastic instability and is valid only for long, slender columns (high slenderness ratio).

q: 21. The Rankine's formula holds good for
explain: Rankine's empirical formula was developed specifically to bridge the gap between crushing (short column) and buckling (long column) failure, making it applicable across both ranges.

q: 22. In case of eccentrically loaded struts ............. is preferred
explain: For eccentrically loaded struts, a composite section is preferred as it can be tailored (e.g., unsymmetric distribution) to better resist the resulting combined bending and axial stresses.

q: 23. The stress at which the extension of the material takes place more quickly as compared to the increase in load, is called
explain: This describes the yield point, where strain increases disproportionately compared to the increase in load/stress.

q: 24. The stress developed in the material without any permanent set is called
explain: The elastic limit is defined as the maximum stress up to which the material returns to its original shape completely (no permanent set) after unloading.

q: 25. The tensile test is carried on ............. materials.
explain: Tensile tests (measuring elongation, necking, ductile yielding behavior) are primarily meaningful and carried out on ductile materials.

q: 26. The compression test is carried on ............. materials.
explain: Compression tests are the standard test method for brittle materials (like cast iron, concrete), which are weak in tension but strong in compression.

q: 27. Factor of safety is defined as the ratio of
explain: Factor of safety is standardly defined as the ratio of the ultimate (or yield) stress to the permissible working stress used in design.

q: 28. The ratio of lateral strain to axial strain of a homogenous material is known as
explain: By definition, Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to axial (longitudinal) strain.

q: 29. The normal and tangential components of stress on an inclined plane through to the direction of the force will be equal to
explain: For a uniaxial stress acting on an inclined plane, the normal and tangential (shear) stress components become equal when the plane is inclined at 45° to the force direction.

q: 30. The locus of the end point of the resultant of the normal and tangential components of the stress on an inclined plane is
explain: As the inclination of the plane varies, the resultant stress vector's endpoint traces out an ellipse (the stress ellipse), similar to the momental ellipse for inertia.

q: 31. Principal planes are subjected to
options: normal stresses as well as tangential stresses
explain: By definition, a principal plane carries only normal stress with zero shear (tangential) stress.

q: 32. The maximum shear stress will always occur at
options: a fibre in the cross-section depending on the configuration
explain: While maximum shear stress is at the neutral axis for symmetric sections like rectangles and circles, for unsymmetrical sections (like T-sections) it can occur elsewhere, so it depends on the section's configuration.

q: 33. In an I section almost all the shear force is taken by
options: half the depth of each flange
explain: In an I-section, due to its geometry, the thin web carries the vast majority (typically over 90%) of the total shear force, while the flanges carry very little.

q: 34. Twisting moment is a moment applied in the plane of cross-section acting about
explain: Twisting (torsional) moment acts about the longitudinal axis of the member, causing rotation of cross-sections relative to each other.

q: 35. If a shaft is subjected to pure twisting moment, an element on the surface is subjected to
explain: Under pure torsion, an element on the surface of a shaft experiences pure shear stress (with associated principal stresses at 45° being tension/compression).

q: 36. A brittle material will
options: never be used for structural purposes
explain: Brittle materials fracture suddenly with little to no prior plastic deformation or visible warning, unlike ductile materials.

q: 37. Glass will obey Hooke's law up to
explain: Being a brittle material with no distinct yield point, glass behaves elastically (obeying Hooke's law) right up until sudden fracture.

q: 38. The effect of the size of the specimen on ultimate strength will be more serious for
explain: Brittle materials are more sensitive to flaws/defects that scale with specimen size, so size effects on ultimate strength are more pronounced for brittle materials.

q: 39. If a material has identical properties in all directions, it is said to be
explain: Isotropic means having identical mechanical properties in every direction at a point, as opposed to homogeneous (uniform properties throughout the material, but possibly directionally dependent).

q: 40. When a member is subjected to axial tensile load, the greatest normal stress is equal to
explain: Under uniaxial tension σ, the maximum shear stress is σ/2, so the greatest normal stress (σ) is twice the maximum shear stress.

q: 41. Hooke's law states that stress and strain are
explain: Hooke's law states that within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain.

q: 42. A shaft is subjected to bending moment M and a torque T simultaneously. The ratio of the maximum bending stress to maximum shear stress developed in the shaft is
explain: Comparing bending stress (σ = 32M/πd³) to shear stress (τ = 16T/πd³) for a circular shaft gives a ratio σ/τ = 2M/T.

q: 43. The greatest load which a spring can carry without getting permanently distorted is called
explain: Proof load is defined as the maximum load a spring can withstand without undergoing permanent deformation.

q: 44. Limit of proportionality depends upon
explain: The limit of proportionality (where Hooke's law ceases to apply) is an intrinsic material property, depending on the type of material rather than its geometry or loading type.

q: 45. If the Young's modulus of elasticity of a material is twice of its modulus of rigidity, the Poisson's ratio of the material is
explain: Using E = 2G(1+μ), if E = 2G, then 2G = 2G(1+μ), giving 1+μ=1, so μ = 0 (zero).

q: 46. For an isotropic, homogenous and elastic material obeying Hooke's law, number of independent elastic constant is
explain: For an isotropic homogeneous elastic material, only 2 independent elastic constants (e.g., E and G, or E and Poisson's ratio) are needed, since all others can be derived from these.

q: 47. A close coil helical spring when subjected to a moment M having its axis along the axis of helix is
options: it is subjected to pure bending
its number of coil will increase
explain: When a closed-coil spring is subjected to a moment about its own (helix) axis, the wire experiences pure bending (as opposed to axial loading which causes torsion).

q: 48. The stress below which a material has a high probability of not failing under reversal of stress is known as
explain: The endurance limit (fatigue limit) is defined as the maximum stress below which a material can withstand an infinite number of stress reversals (cycles) without fatigue failure.

q: 49. In a rectangular shaft subjected to torsion, the maximum shear stress occurs at
explain: For a rectangular (non-circular) shaft under torsion, the maximum shear stress occurs at the midpoint of the longer side, per membrane analogy/torsion theory for non-circular sections.

q: 50. The specimen in Charpy impact test is supported as a
explain: In the Charpy impact test, the notched specimen is supported horizontally at both ends (as a simply supported beam) and struck at the center opposite the notch.
